findings.description: AWS access key and secret access key are embedded in plaintext in the EC2 user_data script, which is visible to anyone with access to the instance metadata or the Terraform state, leading to credential leakage.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true (and the encrypted attribute is commented out), meaning data at rest on this volume is stored unencrypted.

The snapshot is taken from an unencrypted EBS volume and has no encryption configured itself, so the resulting snapshot data is stored unencrypted, exposing potentially sensitive data if the snapshot is shared or leaked.
The security group allows inbound TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH management access to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.
The security group allows inbound TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 with no additional protections (e.g., WAF, TLS termination), exposing the web service in cleartext to the entire internet.

map_public_ip_on_launch = true automatically assigns public IP addresses to instances launched in this subnet, increasing exposure of the web host (which also has SSH and HTTP open to the world) to the public internet.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true automatically assigns public IP addresses to any instance launched in this subnet, expanding the network attack surface unnecessarily.

The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration) defined, leaving potentially sensitive network flow log data unencrypted at rest.

The S3 bucket has no public access block or bucket policy restricting access, and force_destroy is enabled; without explicit access restrictions the bucket could be publicly reachable depending on account-level settings, exposing flow log data.
